[[File:神道修成派大元祠 worship hall (upper shrine).jpg|thumb|right|The worship hall of the upper shrine of {{nihongo|Shintō Shūseiha Daigenshi|神道修成派大元祠|}} on the summit of {{nihongo|Mount Shishigahana|獅子ケ鼻山}} in [[Iwata, Shizuoka]]]]
{{nihongo|'''Nitta Kuniteru'''|新田邦光}} (1829–1902) was a founder of a [[Sect Shinto]] group. He founded {{nihongo|[[Shinto Shusei]]|神道修成派|Shintō shūsei-ha}} in 1849.<ref name="國學院大學デジタルミュージアム2">{{Cite web |date=2023-03-06 |title=Nitta Kuniteru {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム |url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9482 |access-date=2023-11-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230306212657/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9482 |archive-date=2023-03-06 }}</ref>  He read the [[Analects]] at age 9.<ref name="國學院大學デジタルミュージアム2" /> He founded the sect at age twenty,<ref name="國學院大學デジタルミュージアム2" /> and considered Japanese people to be descendants of deities.<ref name="國學院大學デジタルミュージアム2" /> He considered allegiance to the [[Emperor of Japan]] to be central to his philosophy; he was a supporter of [[Sonnō jōi]] but supported the [[Boshin War|Boshin Rebellion]] and the [[Meiji Restoration]] later.<ref name="國學院大學デジタルミュージアム2" /><ref name="Glossary-of-Shinto-Names-and-Terms-2023a">{{Cite web |date=2023-03-10 |title=Glossary of Shinto Names and Terms: Shintô shûsei-ha |url=https://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/ijcc/wp/glossary/def_S.html |access-date=2023-11-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230310074817/https://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/ijcc/wp/glossary/def_S.html |archive-date=2023-03-10 }}</ref> He managed to gain independence for the sect in 1876.<ref name="Glossary-of-Shinto-Names-and-Terms-2023a" />

He believed that man's body came from his parents but his spirit came from the three kami [[Ame-no-Minakanushi]], [[Takamimusubi]], and [[Kamimusubi]] who he identified with [[Shangdi]]. His sect had very positive attitudes towards science and commerce.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kitagawa |first=Joseph M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lani3dFCC9UC&dq=Nitta+Kuniteru&pg=PA217 |title=Religion in Japanese History |date=1990-11-21 |publisher=Columbia University Press |isbn=978-0-231-51509-2 |language=en}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Nitta Kuniteru was born on December 30, 1829. His birthplace was Ebara-mura (拝原村) in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa Province]] on the island of [[Shikoku]] (present-day [[Mima, Tokushima]]). He had several names. Sometimes he was called Takezawa Kansaburo. He also used the name Toyō.<ref name="Holtom-2012a">{{Cite book |last=Holtom |first=D. C. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Tk2X6zGpKQwC&dq=Nitta+Kuniteru&pg=PA206 |title=National Faith Of Japan: A Study in Modern Shinto |date=2012-11-12 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-136-16564-1 |language=en}}</ref>

He read the [[Analects]] at age 9 in 1838.<ref name="國學院大學デジタルミュージアム2" /> 

Kuniteru believed Japan was a sacred land. He thought the people were descendants of gods from an early age.<ref name="Inoue-2003a">{{Cite book |last1=Inoue |first1=Nobutaka |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XGY4xPDRDQgC&dq=Nitta+Kuniteru&pg=PA178 |title=Shinto: A Short History |last2=Jun |first2=Endo |last3=Mizue |first3=Mori |last4=Satoshi |first4=Ito |date=2003-09-02 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-134-38462-4 |language=en}}</ref>

His early life was a time of change during the late [[Edo period]]. There was unrest in the country. Western ideas and Christian missions were influencing Japan. This worried many people. They wanted to protect Japanese culture.<ref name="Holtom-2012a" />

Nitta Kuniteru thought deeply about these issues. He believed in Shinto, the traditional religion of Japan, but he combined it with Confucian philosophy. He traveled around Japan. He talked to people about his ideas. He wanted to unite the [[Japanese people]]. He was against foreign influences.<ref name="Holtom-2012a" /> He founded the sect at the age of 20 in 1849.<ref name="國學院大學デジタルミュージアム2" /> 

He was involved in politics. He supported the Emperor and [[Sonnō jōi]] the movement to restore the emperor. This was during the end of the Tokugawa regime. He believed religion was important for a strong country. He promoted his own version of [[Confucian Shinto]]. He went to places controlled by the Tokugawa. He told people to follow the Emperor. This led to his arrest. Later, he was released. He then lived in [[Edo]], which is now Tokyo.<ref name="Holtom-2012a" />

In 1868, Kuniteru joined the [[Department of Divinities]]. This was a government office for Shinto rituals. He got involved in a scandal. This led to his imprisonment in the [[Oshi Domain|Oshi domain]].<ref name="Inoue-2003a" />

In [[Edo]], he continued preaching about nationalism. His ideas were popular and he gained a large following.<ref name="Inoue-2003a" /> On August 31, 1873, they formed the Shusei Association. This group became a new Shinto sect.<ref name="Holtom-2012a" /> He managed to gain independence for the sect in 1876.<ref name="Glossary-of-Shinto-Names-and-Terms-2023a" /><ref name="Holtom-2012a" /><ref name="Inoue-2003a" /> Kuniteru became the first leader of this sect in 1884.<ref name="Holtom-2012a" /><ref name="Inoue-2003a" />

Kuniteru's teachings are a distinct form of [[Confucian Shinto]] from the older [[Suika Shinto]]. This approach attracted more followers. He also welcomed members from other religious groups. These included the [[Ontake-kyō|Ontake]] and [[mountain worship]] Shinto sects.<ref name="Inoue-2003a" />

He died on November 25, 1902. [[Shinto Shusei]] still exists today and is headquartered in [[Iwata, Shizuoka]].<ref name="Holtom-2012a" />
